statement: BASS-II hypothesis: with adequate ventilation, materials in microgravity burn as well as or better than in normal gravity at the same pressure, O2 and temperature, so NASA's upward-burning Test 1 - the worst case on Earth - may not be conservative in space.
caveat: this is the stated hypothesis, not a result

statement: BASS-II experiment table: 129 runs (2014-02-14 to 2018-06-24) at initial O2 of 13.6-22.2%. Tested O2 ranges by sample: clear PMMA rods 13.6-22.2% (28 runs), SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric 16.4-20.8% (27), black rods 15.4-20.8% (26), PMMA films 15.0-22.2% (22), PMMA slabs 17.9-22.2% (20).
source_ref: runs.csv, psi_id = PSI-25 (o2_pct by fuel and fuel_geometry)
caveat: ranges of conditions tested, not flammability limits: the table has no burn / no-burn column

statement: Lowest-oxygen BASS-II run: a 3/8-inch clear PMMA rod at 13.6% O2 (label O12) carries the remark that it did not ignite at any flow.
caveat: single run; remark taken from the table as written

statement: A microgravity flammability boundary for PMMA rods in axial stagnation flow was mapped from BASS-II runs (clear and black rods, flow 0-55 cm/s, O2 13.6-22.2%); at the high-flow side the flame blows off, starting as a hole in the flame sheet at the stagnation region.
source_ref: PSI-25-P01: Olson & Ferkul, Combustion and Flame (2017)
caveat: abstract only, full paper not read

statement: BASS-II flame extinctions indicate that materials (PMMA rods, sheets and slabs, cotton-fiberglass fabric) can burn at a lower oxygen concentration in microgravity than in normal gravity; the authors propose a normal-gravity test method that could account for partial gravity and say more research is needed there.
source_ref: Olson, Ferkul, Fernandez-Pello, Miller, ICES 2019 (not in the PSI-25 publication list)
caveat: abstract only

statement: Opposed-flow flame spread over PMMA rods was sustained at a lower oxygen level in microgravity (17%) than in normal gravity (18%) and could be faster, implying a higher fire risk under some conditions; exploration atmospheres with lower pressure and higher O2 raise it further.
source_ref: Scientific Reports 2017/2018 paper using BASS-II opposed-flow rod data (not matched to a PSI publication row)
caveat: abstract only

statement: Normal-gravity counterpart of the BASS-II rod tests (same geometry, upward stagnation flow): the 1-g blowoff boundary is linear, with oxygen concentration proportional to flow speed - the basis for a ground test that estimates low-gravity flammability.
caveat: abstract only

statement: BASS-II varied airflow from 0 to 55 cm/s at 21% O2 and below. For thin PMMA in opposed flow the report gives radiative quenching at very low flow (below about 2 cm/s) and blowoff near 40 cm/s for a 0.1 mm sample; with BASS-I, well over one hundred tests were run.
source_ref: Combustion of Solids in Microgravity: Results from the BASS-II Experiment, NTRS 20160000593
caveat: from presentation slides; oxygen level for the quoted limits not recorded

statement: BASS: Ultem and Nomex HT90-40 did not burn at 21-22% O2 with about 15 cm/s flow, while Nomex-III did; flames quenched when flow fell to about 1 cm/s, and spread rate rose linearly with flow speed.
caveat: abstract-level reading; sample for the quenching and spread-rate statements not recorded

statement: BASS experiment table: 121 rows (2012-03-30 to 2013-06-01): PMMA 69 (50 rows are spheres), SIBAL fabric 12, wax and candle samples 23, Nomex 6, Ultem 2, 9 without a material. The table gives no oxygen level or flow speed per run.
caveat: per-run conditions are probably in 'As Run_Test Matrix.xlsx' (files.csv), not parsed

statement: Saffire-II table: all four silicone samples (0.27-1.03 mm, 20 cm/s) showed about zero burn length in microgravity, although in 1-g two of them burned completely and one burned 7.6 cm.
caveat: one flow speed, one sample each; opposite direction to the BASS-II trend for PMMA

statement: Saffire-II table: both SIBAL cotton-fiberglass samples burned the full 29 cm in microgravity at 2.1 and 2.6 mm/s; the PMMA section of a PMMA/Nomex sample was consumed but the Nomex did not ignite; two thick PMMA samples burned for 600 and 900 s with the flame anchored at the sample base (regression 0.01-0.04 mm/s).
source_ref: runs.csv, psi_id = PSI-99 (samples 2-5 to 2-9) and table notes

statement: Saffire-I table: the same 94 x 40.6 cm SIBAL sheet burned for 420 s in concurrent flow and 70 s in opposed flow at 20 cm/s and about 21.5% O2. Saffire-III repeated it at 30 cm/s, but its table gives no burn times.
caveat: burn time only; spread rates are in the raw data

statement: Saffire rationale: fire behaves so differently in reduced gravity that designing spacecraft fire safety from terrestrial fires and standards carries inherent risk, and microgravity data for designers are scarce - hence large burns in an uncrewed Cygnus vehicle.
caveat: stated hypothesis

statement: BRE (preliminary, as stated on the page): quasi-steady burning corresponding to condensed fuels such as PMMA and Nylon was observed in microgravity with no air flow, notably in elevated-oxygen atmospheres planned for future spacecraft, whereas flames in 21% O2 went out by themselves quickly. Stopping ventilation may therefore not be enough.
caveat: page calls the results preliminary

statement: BRE test log: 194 flames ignited on 18 test days (Feb 2019 - Jan 2021) with ethylene and methane on 25 mm and 50 mm porous burners at 21, 25, 26.5, 34 and 40% O2; objectives name the exploration atmospheres 14.7 psia / 21%, 10.2 psia / 26.5% and 8.2 psia / 34% O2.
source_ref: test_matrix.csv, psi_id = PSI-20; PSI-20 page, Objective
caveat: per-day summary; pressure and outcome per flame are only in the raw data

statement: Ground modelling of BASS / BASS-II (unsteady flamelet-generated manifolds plus two-colour tomography of flight images) aims to reproduce the 'Goldilocks' flammability zone reported by Olson and Ferkul, i.e. burning only within a band of flow speeds.
caveat: aim, not a result; the record holds no data files

statement: NASA Glenn's combustion-science page lists FM2, SoFIE and FLARE as current investigations and ACME, BASS, DAFT, FLEX, Saffire, SAME, SLICE and SPICE as archived, and notes that the normal-gravity NASA-STD-6001 flammability test may not be conservative for low gravity.
caveat: CFI is not on that page; page read 2026-11-15

statement: SAME / SAME-R hypothesis: without buoyant flow, smoke from overheated materials grows into larger particles than in 1-g (higher vapour concentration and longer residence time near the source), with lower number density - which changes detector response and may leave some detectors silent.
caveat: stated hypothesis

statement: SAME findings (fact sheet): significant mass in particles larger than 1 micron; Teflon smoke mostly below 1 micron; all materials give sub-micron particles best seen by ionization detectors; light scattering works for most cases; detection should target pre-fire heating products rather than soot.
source_ref: NASA fact sheet: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)
caveat: carried over from the earlier draft; not checked against the SAME final report in PSI

statement: SAME planned matrix: Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, lampwick and dibutyl phthalate, each at air flow 5 or 10 cm/s, weight-loss rate 1 or 2 mg/min and smoke aging of 1 or 20 min.
caveat: planned conditions, no measured sizes in the table

statement: SAME-R was flown because all SAME TEM grids came back contaminated. Changes: Pyrell foam replaced DBP, higher heating temperatures and no-flow heating were added, and a GRC-built M-pass instrument replaced one commercial enclosure. 66 test points were run 16 Jul - 9 Sep 2010, followed by ground tests of the log-normal assumption.

SAME-R table: 109 rows (42 aged-smoke rows): Kapton 29, silicone 22, lampwick 20, Pyrell 20, Teflon 18; inlet velocity 8.1 cm/s in 74 rows and 0 in 22; heater ratio Rt/R0 1.22-1.48; aging from tens of seconds to more than 800 s.
caveat: conditions only; measured particle sizes are in the Analyzed Data spreadsheets (not parsed)

statement: DAFT: the TSI P-Trak particle counter relies on gravity to recycle isopropanol and was expected to clog or over-count in microgravity; a capillary condenser and removal of the orientation switch were tested on ISS in 2005 against a DustTrak with an Arizona Road Dust aerosol. Fact sheet: ISS particulate levels were low compared with the Shuttle and particles were larger than on Earth.
source_ref: PSI-47 page (Objective, Approach, Hypothesis) and experiment table; NASA DAFT fact sheet
caveat: the PSI page itself gives no results

statement: Ground simulation of SAME: DNS of dibutyl-phthalate smoke at two low cross-flow speeds compares particle size distributions in 1-g and microgravity through thermophoresis, settling and wake geometry.
caveat: no quantitative result on the page; final report not read

statement: Spinoff 1978 'Fire Detector': an air-sampling sensor derived from the incipient fire detector used in Space Shuttle orbiters distinguishes combustion particles from dust, warns before flame or smoke appears, and can be networked to locate a fire in large sites such as mines.
FLEX table: 274 droplet tests (2009-03-05 to 2011-12-08; heptane 117, methanol 157) at O2 12-34% and 0.69-3.05 atm. Outcomes: flame extinguished 186, test disrupted 61, burned to completion 27.

FLEX suppressant coverage: CO2 added in 123 tests (mole fraction up to 0.70), helium in 50 (up to 0.45), none in 101. Share burning to completion: heptane 10 of 47 without suppressant, 3 of 48 with CO2, 6 of 22 with He; methanol 3 of 54, 5 of 75 and 0 of 28.
caveat: O2 and droplet size differ between groups, so the shares are descriptive, not a controlled comparison

statement: FLEX burning-rate column: mean 0.545 for heptane (107 values, 0.05-1.06) and 0.472 for methanol (151 values, 0.20-0.74).
caveat: unit is not stated in the table; magnitude fits a burning-rate constant in mm2/s (inferred)

statement: FLEX discovery: after the visible hot flame of a large n-alkane droplet went out by radiative extinction, the droplet kept burning quasi-steadily with a cool flame, which then ended abruptly at a finite droplet diameter.
source_ref: PSI-69-P34: Nayagam et al., Combustion and Flame (2012); NASA report NTRS 20140006750
caveat: abstracts only

statement: First FLEX results: as ambient oxygen was reduced, the droplet diameter at diffusive extinction increased and the diameter at radiative extinction decreased; the limiting oxygen index is the fire-safety measure derived from these tests.
source_ref: Dietrich et al., Microgravity Science and Technology (2014)
caveat: abstract only

statement: Fire-safety implication of cool flames: because cool-flame burning persists after the hot flame is out, safety procedures based only on hot flames may be inadequate.
source_ref: Nayagam, APS Ohio-Region Section plenary abstract (April 2021)
caveat: conference abstract

statement: CFI table: 87 rows (79 unique tests, 9 Mar - 21 Aug 2017) with n-dodecane (22) and n-dodecane/iso-dodecane 60/40 (41) and 75/25 (24) at 0.5-5 atm; O2 0.21 in 63 rows and 0.17 in 24; helium 0.29 or 0.59 in 14 rows.
caveat: conditions only; outcomes are in 'CFI_DataSummary_Spreadsheet_Jan2021.xlsx' (not parsed)

statement: Counterflow study built on FLEX data: the warm flame has a double reaction zone and mediates the transition between cool and hot flames; at elevated pressure the flammable region of warm and cool flames widens.
caveat: ground experiments and simulation

statement: FLEX-2 in PSI offers a planned matrix only: 8 fuels (iso-octane, n-octane, heptane, decane, ethanol, two propanol/glycerol blends, heptane/iso-octane), droplets 1.5-5 mm, O2 0.17-0.30 in N2 or He, 0.5-3 atm, flow 0.1-5 cm/s.
caveat: no per-run outcomes

statement: CFI-G table: 333 flames (179 normal, 154 inverse; butane 140, propane 99, ethane 94) at O2 12-85% and 0.49-3.27 atm. Outcomes: hot flame 256, no ignition 59, cool flame recorded 9, flash 8, unknown 1.

All 9 cool flames in the CFI-G table are normal n-butane flames: 5 on day 21174 (23 June 2021) and 2 on day 21291, at 2 atm, about 39-40% O2 and 30% butane; 2 on day 21106 at 0.5 atm, about 35% O2 and 50% butane, noted as igniting directly as cool flames.
caveat: ethane, propane and all inverse flames show no cool flame in the table

statement: Spherical cool diffusion flames burning gases were observed for the first time; they were hard to produce and appeared only for normal flames (n-butane, 2 bar, O2 mole fraction about 0.39); burner temperature is important to their behaviour.
source_ref: PSI-159-P01: Kim et al., Proc. Combust. Inst. (2023)
caveat: abstract only

statement: Between January and June 2021 more than 150 hot diffusion flames were burned without any hot-to-cool transition; on 23 June 2021, after the hot flame went out, residual burner heat re-ignited the fuel as a steady cool flame (n-butane in N2, 40% O2, 2 atm). Cool flames burn at about 600-1000 K.
source_ref: University of Maryland news and press release (July 2021); NASA article on CFI-G
caveat: university news item; the release counts three such tests, the PSI table flags five on that day

statement: Flame Design tables: 207 normal flames (25 Apr 2019 - 28 Oct 2021; ethylene 187, propane 20) at ambient O2 19.8-40%, 0.93-1.30 atm, adiabatic flame temperature 1683-2831 K; 120 inverse flames (24 Nov 2021 - 11 Feb 2022) with burner O2 21.2-85% at 0.43-3.01 atm, 2074-2974 K.
caveat: conditions only: no soot or extinction outcome per test

statement: Flame Design hypotheses: soot needs local C/O ratio and temperature above critical values together with low strain rate; microgravity spherical diffusion flames go out when the peak temperature first drops below 1130 K; steady spherical diffusion flames are possible.
caveat: hypotheses; results are in the final report (not read)

statement: ACME day-level logs record 1,033 ignited flames: BRE 194 (18 days), CLD Flame 344 (32 days), E-FIELD Flames 219 (20 days), s-Flame 276 (18 days).
caveat: the PSI pages give day summaries, not per-flame conditions

statement: CLD Flame (fact sheet): microgravity coflow flames are taller, wider and cooler with 5-8 times more soot than in 1-g; weak flames are more stable and dilution limits extend.
source_ref: NASA fact sheet: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME)
caveat: carried over from the earlier draft; the PSI page states goals only

statement: E-FIELD Flames applied up to 10 kV between burner and a mesh electrode to methane and ethylene flames (219 flames, both polarities, coflow and gas-jet burners). The page states the work is not aimed at space applications; the benefit is emission and soot control on Earth.
source_ref: PSI-22 page, Approach and Research Impacts; test_matrix.csv
caveat: no results on the page

statement: s-Flame targets transient structure, convective and radiative extinction limits and pulsating instabilities of spherical flames; 276 flames with H2, CH4, C2H4 and H2/CH4 blends in about 21% or 30% O2 with N2 or He dilution.
caveat: no results on the page

statement: SPICE table: 469 rows over 11 GMT days: propylene 75% (135), propylene (122), propylene 50% (111), propane (50), ethylene (47), methane (4); nozzles 1.6 mm (178 rows), 0.41 mm (172), 0.76 mm (119). The page reports 526 flames and coflow of 5.4-65 cm/s.
source_ref: runs.csv, psi_id = PSI-107; PSI-107 page, Approach
caveat: no smoke-point flag and no year in the table

statement: SPICE (fact sheet): 250 tests gave more than 70 smoke points; soot dominates the heat emitted by the flames.
source_ref: NASA fact sheet: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE)
caveat: test count differs from the PSI page (526 flames) and table (469 rows)

statement: Ground analysis of SPICE images (more than 1,600 raw frames, colour-ratio pyrometry) starts from the hypothesis that microgravity flames are longer, more diffuse, cooler and sootier than in 1-g.
caveat: hypothesis; the record holds no data files

statement: SLICE: more than 4,000 still images over 12 listed test days (9 Feb - 23 Mar 2012) of methane and ethylene coflow flames, used to find lift-off limits and dilution effects.
caveat: no results on the page; table lists days and fuels only

statement: Apollo 1 (27 Jan 1967): fire in a 100% oxygen cabin during a ground test that had been classed as non-hazardous; probable source was electrical arcing near environmental-control wiring; the hatch needed about 90 s to open and the crew died of asphyxia from carbon monoxide. The redesign brought a unified quick-opening hatch (about 3 s) and limits on combustible materials.
source_ref: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance, Apollo 1 lessons
caveat: from notes taken when the page was read

statement: Apollo 13: oxygen tank heater switches rated for 28 V were not updated when ground power rose to 65 V DC; during a long detanking (about 8 h) heater temperatures reached about 1000 F and damaged Teflon wire insulation, which led to the explosion of oxygen tank 2 in flight.
source_ref: NASA Safety and Mission Assurance, Apollo 13 lessons
caveat: from notes taken when the page was read

statement: Mir (24 Feb 1997): a solid-fuel oxygen generator canister (lithium perchlorate) caught fire in the Kvant-1 module with six people aboard; smoke took hours to clear. NASA describes it as the most serious fire aboard an orbiting spacecraft.
source_ref: NASA History: 25 Years Ago - Fire Aboard Space Station Mir
caveat: from notes taken when the page was read

statement: Spinoff 1976 'Fireman's Air Tanks': Scott Aviation with Johnson Space Center built a breathing set of about 20 lb - 13 lb lighter than conventional tanks - giving 30 minutes of air at 4,500 psi from a composite-wrapped aluminium cylinder.

Spinoff 1982 'New Technology for the Fire Attire' (Project FIRES): lightweight fire- and heat-resistant materials from spacesuits and spacecraft thermal protection were used for a firefighter ensemble, co-sponsored by NASA and the U.S. Fire Administration, managed by Marshall, field-tested by 14 fire departments.
source_ref: NASA Spinoff 1982, New Technology for the Fire Attire

statement: NASA's Researcher's Guide to ISS combustion science (e-book, October 2015) is the general reference for facilities and experiment families; a copy also sits in the BRE and E-FIELD Science Documents folders in PSI.
source_ref: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science

statement: No partial-gravity (Moon, Mars) data: all 1,862 runs in runs.csv are microgravity (ISS or Cygnus). The BASS-II team itself says partial-gravity flammability needs more research.
caveat: limited to the 24 combustion records in PSI

psi_ids: PSI-10; PSI-107; PSI-39; PSI-101; PSI-26; PSI-25
statement: Outcome per run exists only for CFI-G (333), FLEX (274) and Saffire-I/II (11). Flame Design, SPICE, CFI and SAME-R tables give conditions only, and the BASS / BASS-II tables have no burn / no-burn column.
caveat: outcomes may be recoverable from xlsx files listed in files.csv

psi_ids: PSI-20; PSI-21; PSI-22; PSI-23; PSI-106; PSI-68; PSI-102; PSI-47
statement: Eight flight investigations have no per-run table on PSI at all: four ACME experiments and SLICE give day summaries, FLEX-2 and SAME give planned matrices, DAFT lists two sessions.
caveat: per-run conditions would have to come from raw data

statement: Suppression agents are thinly covered: FLEX adds CO2 or helium to the ambient and BASS used nitrogen (fact sheet). None of the 24 combustion records describes tests of water mist, foam or other extinguisher agents.
source_ref: PSI pages of the 24 combustion investigations (objective and approach)
caveat: based on page text, not on the raw data or publications

statement: Ground records PSI-62 and PSI-60 contain only a metadata archive (no data files); PSI-115 has data and a final report but no publications.
Raw data volume is about 13.5 TB in 66,567 files across the 24 records; nothing was downloaded - files.csv holds folder totals and links to 177 light files.
SoFIE, FLARE, FM2, BASS-M and Saffire-IV to VI are not in the PSI combustion search results, so the dataset has only context rows for them.
caveat: PSI search checked 2026-11-15: 24 combustion records

statement: The PSI API gives no publication year: only 13 of 352 publication rows carry one.
caveat: years can be filled from DOIs (293 rows have a DOI)

statement: Saffire-I record: investigation dates (2001-2008) and proposal title are identical to the SAME record, and the platform is listed as ISS although the burn was in Cygnus.

CFI record: page dates are 2020-10-01 to 2021-10-20 but the table tests are March-August 2017; approach text says 0.25-0.5 atm while the objective says 0.25-5 atm and the table spans 0.5-5 atm; 8 table rows are duplicates.
Row counts disagree with page text: BASS 121 table rows vs 89 test points; BASS-II 129 vs 130; SPICE 469 vs 526 flames; SAME-R 109 rows vs 66 test points (aged-smoke rows are separate).

ACME summary tables carry spreadsheet artefacts: O2 cells '3400%' and '2100%' (BRE), bottle labels incremented to 'CH5' ... 'C2H11' (CLD Flame), 'N3' ... 'N6' (s-Flame), and a duplicated last block (E-FIELD).
source_ref: experiment tables; raw copies in runs_raw/
caveat: normalised in test_matrix.csv, raw text kept

statement: Saffire sample thickness is given in cm in the Saffire-I and III tables (0.37, .33) but the same fabric is 0.37 mm in Saffire-II; stored as mm. Saffire-I length and width are swapped relative to the page text.
caveat: unit correction is an inference

statement: Column meanings checked: TFP (CFI-G) most likely means thin-filament pyrometry; BASS-II air display is in cm/s and the fan display mixes fan and potentiometer settings; the FLEX column headed CO holds CO2.
source_ref: experiment tables; PSI-10 keywords; PSI-21 approach; Kim et al. abstract
caveat: TFP is not defined on the PSI-159 page

statement: Missing or inconsistent record metadata: licence blank (PSI-10); investigation dates blank (SPICE, SLICE) or ending before the last tests (s-Flame); end date blank (Saffire-III); sub-area and hardware blank (SLICE).
Publication lists overlap between records: 352 rows correspond to about 287 distinct papers; 62 rows repeat a paper listed under another investigation.
caveat: matching by DOI or normalised title
